name: Washington, D.C.
kicker: Capital of the United States since 1800 · Federal district on the Potomac
briefing: Washington, D.C., is the capital of the United States, but it is not part of any state. The Residence Act of 1790 put the capital on the Potomac River, George Washington picked the exact spot, and Pierre L’Enfant designed a city of wide avenues, while Benjamin Banneker helped survey its borders. The government moved there in 1800, and British troops burned the Capitol and the White House during the War of 1812.
answerHtml: Washington, D.C. (accept District of Columbia or D.C.; do not accept “Washington State” or “George Washington”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Residence Act of 1790 called for building this city along the Potomac River. Its location came out of a deal made at a dinner hosted by Thomas Jefferson, in which Alexander Hamilton won Southern votes for his plan to take over the states’ war debts.
tossups.r: Philadelphia served as the temporary capital until the government moved here in 1800. For 10 points, name this capital city of the United States.

tossups.p: A French-born engineer who had fought in the Continental Army drew this city’s plan of wide avenues cutting diagonally across a grid, but he was fired in 1792 after clashing with officials. In 1909, his remains were reburied at Arlington National Cemetery on a hill overlooking this city.
tossups.r: That engineer was Pierre L’Enfant [“lahn-FAHN”]. For 10 points, name this capital city on the Potomac River.

tossups.p: A self-taught astronomer who later sent Thomas Jefferson a copy of his almanac, along with a letter challenging Jefferson’s views on race, helped Andrew Ellicott survey this city’s borders in 1791. Many of the boundary stones from that survey, set about a mile apart, still stand.
tossups.r: That man was Benjamin Banneker. For 10 points, name this federal city laid out on land from Maryland and Virginia.

tossups.p: A day after enemy troops set fire to this city, a violent storm that included a tornado swept through it and helped put out the flames. Those troops had marched in after routing American militia at Bladensburg, Maryland, in August 1814.
tossups.r: Dolley Madison had a famous portrait of the first president saved before the White House burned. For 10 points, name this city that British troops burned during the War of 1812.

tossups.p: Residents of this city first voted for president in 1964, after the 23rd Amendment gave it electoral votes. That 1961 amendment says this city can never have more electors than the least populous state, so it has three.
tossups.r: Its delegate in the House cannot vote on final passage of bills. For 10 points, name this federal district, the capital of the United States.

tossups.p: A British scientist who never visited the United States left his fortune to found an institution of learning in this city, and in 1904 Alexander Graham Bell brought that scientist’s remains here from Italy. That institution’s red sandstone “Castle” stands on the National Mall.
tossups.r: That institution is the Smithsonian. For 10 points, name this capital city, home to the National Air and Space Museum.

tossups.p: In 1846, Congress gave back to Virginia the part of this capital’s original ten-mile square that lay across the Potomac, including the port of Alexandria. That land includes Arlington, where the Pentagon and Arlington National Cemetery were later built.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal district that originally took land from both Virginia and Maryland.

tossups.p: Every April 16, this city celebrates Emancipation Day, marking an 1862 law that freed enslaved people here about nine months before the Emancipation Proclamation. That law paid slaveholders who were loyal to the Union for each person freed.
tossups.r: The Compromise of 1850 had already banned the slave trade, but not slavery, here. For 10 points, name this capital city.

tossups.p: Many license plates in this city carry a protest slogan about “taxation without representation,” because its residents pay federal taxes but have no voting member of Congress. The Home Rule Act of 1973 allowed its residents to elect a mayor and a council.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal district, the capital of the United States, which is not part of any state.

tossups.p: In 1912, the mayor of Tokyo, Yukio Ozaki, sent about three thousand cherry trees to this city, and First Lady Helen Taft planted one of the first two near the Tidal Basin. Each spring, a festival celebrates the blooming of those trees.
tossups.r: Many of those trees stand near the Jefferson Memorial. For 10 points, name this U.S. capital, also home to the Lincoln Memorial.

tossups.p: Construction of an obelisk honoring the first president stopped for more than twenty years, so its marble changes color partway up. When it was finished in 1884, that obelisk in this city was the tallest structure in the world.
tossups.r: It stands on the National Mall between the Capitol and the Lincoln Memorial. For 10 points, name this capital city.

tossups.p: Article One of the Constitution lets Congress rule a district “not exceeding ten miles square” as the seat of government. Thomas Jefferson’s 1801 inauguration was the first held in this city, and John Adams was the first president to live here.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this capital city of the United States, which is not part of any state.

tossups.p: An 1871 law merged this city with Georgetown into a single territorial government, and Alexander “Boss” Shepherd then paved streets and built sewers so quickly that the government ran up huge debts. Congress ended that territorial government in 1874.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this capital city on the Potomac River, whose government Congress controls.

tossups.p: Frederick Douglass spent his last years at Cedar Hill, a house in this city’s Anacostia neighborhood. Bills to make most of this city a state named partly for Douglass passed the House of Representatives in 2020 and 2021 but did not pass the Senate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal district, which has three electoral votes under the 23rd Amendment.

tossups.p: After the Library of Congress burned in 1814, Thomas Jefferson sold his collection of more than six thousand books to restart it. The library’s oldest building, which is named for Jefferson, stands across the street from the Capitol in this city.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city where Pennsylvania Avenue links the Capitol and the White House.

trap.title: City, state, or president?
trap.body: Three different answer lines share this name: George Washington, Washington, D.C., and Washington State. Clues about the Potomac River, L’Enfant’s street plan, the Smithsonian, or the 23rd Amendment want the city; Seattle, Mount Rainier, or Olympia mean the state; and clues about the first president’s life mean George Washington. Arlington National Cemetery and the Pentagon are across the river in Virginia, not in the city.
trap.fix: Listen for “this city,” “this district,” or “this capital.” For the city, “Washington” alone is fine, but if you add anything, make it “D.C.” or “District of Columbia,” never “State.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Washington, D.C. (accept District of Columbia; do not accept “Washington State” or “George Washington”)
